content: Thread spools and other objects on a string can be used to encourage a child to grab, hold, and shake. Colorful cups are useful for activities such as grabbing, holding, banging, dropping, and stacking. A food tin and a large wooden spoon can be used for banging and dropping activities. A plastic jar filled with stones can help a child practice putting objects in and taking them out, as well as counting. A picture drawn or pasted on cardboard can be used as a puzzle for the child to assemble. Books with drawings or magazine pictures can be used to hold and discuss with the child. A stuffed doll with a sewn or painted face can help the child learn about facial features like eyes and nose, tell stories, and provide comfort through holding. When counseling a caregiver about child development, it is important to use play and communication recommendations. Observing the caregiver’s interactions with the child can reveal patterns of sensitive and responsive caregiving. A checklist can guide the counseling process, helping to identify the child’s needs and provide age-appropriate advice. Begin by greeting the caregiver and child in a comfortable setting, such as their home, a clinic, or a community gathering place. Invite the caregiver to sit with the child in a relaxed environment. Sit close, speak softly, and maintain direct eye contact with both the caregiver and the child. Communicate clearly and warmly throughout the session. Ask questions to gather information about the child and the caregiver’s practices, and listen carefully to the caregiver’s responses. These answers will help tailor advice to encourage the child’s development. Focus on the child’s specific needs by observing how the caregiver and child interact. Ask the caregiver about the child’s care practices. Use the checklist to guide the counseling process, ensuring that the advice is appropriate for the child’s age and developmental stage. The checklist also helps assess how the caregiver responds to the child and provides targeted recommendations. For children under six months, ask the caregiver how they play with the baby. If the caregiver moves the baby’s arms and legs or gently strokes the baby, this is a positive interaction. If the caregiver does not play with the baby, discuss ways to stimulate the baby’s senses—sight, hearing, touch, and movement—appropriate for their age. If the caregiver does not talk to the baby, encourage them to make eye contact and speak to the baby. Ask how the caregiver gets the baby to smile, and provide suggestions if needed. For children six months and older, ask how the caregiver plays with the child. If the caregiver does not engage in play, suggest age-appropriate play or communication activities. If the caregiver does not talk to the child or speaks harshly, provide an activity for the caregiver and child to do together. Help the caregiver interpret the child’s actions and thoughts, and encourage them to notice the child’s responses and smiles. Ask how the caregiver encourages the child to smile and provide guidance if necessary. If the caregiver scolds the child, suggest redirecting the child’s attention from unwanted actions by offering an alternative toy or activity. Praise the caregiver for positive practices and provide advice to address any challenges. For example, if the child is slow to learn, encourage more interactive activities and check the child’s hearing and vision. When observing the caregiver and child, note how the caregiver shows awareness of the child’s movements. Many caregivers naturally respond to their child’s moods and movements, such as looking at the child when they walk away or soothing them with a gentle pat on the back. This connection often develops early in life but may be absent due to factors like illness or separation at birth. Fathers who have not had opportunities to bond with their newborns may also struggle to form this connection. Observe how the caregiver comforts the child and shows love. A young child may express discomfort through fussing, crying, or wiggling. Notice whether the child follows the caregiver’s sounds and movements or seeks comfort from them. A caregiver can comfort the child by gently talking, holding, or drawing the child closer. Children who are afraid of new people, places, or sounds may need to be held until they feel safe. Caregivers can help children learn to calm themselves through their reactions, such as using a calm voice instead of loud or threatening noises. When correcting a child, caregivers should avoid harsh scolding or punishment. Instead, they can redirect the child’s attention to safe objects or activities. Young children are easily distracted, so substituting a safe object for a dangerous or inappropriate one can be effective. Over time, children will better understand the reasons behind acceptable and unacceptable behaviors. Caregivers can help children learn what is safe to play with and where. Finally, use the checklist to document observations and interactions. Record the child’s name, age, gender, caregiver’s name, relationship to the child, and address. Note the caregiver’s responses to questions and any advice provided. If necessary, schedule a follow-up visit to reassess the child’s development and the caregiver’s practices.
